Abstract 11

The impact of variable infection risk by race and ethnicity on the dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 spread 12

is largely unknown. Here, we ﬁt structured compartmental models to seroprevalence data from New 13

York State and analyze how herd immunity thresholds (HITs), ﬁnal sizes, and epidemic risk changes 14

across groups. A simple model where interactions occur proportionally to contact rates reduced the 15

HIT, but more realistic models of preferential mixing within groups increased the threshold toward 16

the value observed in homogeneous populations. Across all models, the burden of infection fell dis- 17

proportionately on minority populations: in a model ﬁt to Long Island serosurvey and census data, 18

81% of Hispanics or Latinos were infected when the HIT was reached compared to 34% of non- 19

Hispanic whites. Our ﬁndings, which are meant to be illustrative and not best estimates, demon- 20

strate how racial and ethnic disparities can impact epidemic trajectories and result in unequal distri- 21

butions of SARS-CoV-2 infection. 22

Introduction 23

The dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 spread are inﬂuenced by population heterogeneity. This is especially 24

true for herd immunity, which occurs when susceptible individuals in a population are indirectly pro- 25

tected from infection due to immunity in others. The herd immunity threshold (HIT) is the fraction 26

of the population that is non-susceptible when an unmitigated epidemic reaches its peak, and esti- 27

mating the HIT for SARS-CoV-2 is important for forecasting the harm associated with letting the epi- 28

demic spread in the absence of interventions [1]. A population that has reached the HIT is protected 29

from a new epidemic occurring, until births or waning immunity reduce the proportion nonsuscep- 30

tible below the HIT, but existing cases will still lead to some onward transmission as the epidemic 31

declines and can often result in a ﬁnal epidemic size that exceeds the HIT. In a population with ho- 32

mogeneous mixing, the HIT is 1-1/R0, where R0 is the basic reproduction number; this translates to 33

an HIT of 67% using an R0 of 3. 34

However, population homogeneity is an unrealistic assumption, and models incorporating hetero- 35

geneity in social exposure and infection susceptibility (deﬁned as the probability of infection given 36

exposure) generally result in lowered HITs [2–6]. The key idea behind these models is that sub- 37

populations important for epidemic spread (i.e., those with substantially increased susceptibility or 38

exposure) become infected – and thus develop immunity – early on in an epidemic’s course. Herd 39

immunity for the population overall is then achieved earlier because once these individuals are no 40

longer susceptible to infection, further epidemic spread is slowed. 41

Importantly, these models also imply that in locations where SARS-CoV-2 has spread, there may 42

be demographic sub-populations with particularly high cumulative incidences of infection due to 43

increased exposure, susceptibility, or both. Seroprevalence studies – which characterize past ex- 44

posure by identifying SARS-CoV-2 antibodies – can identify these sub-populations and are more 45

reliable and unbiased than case data, which suffer from under-reporting and other biases [7]. Iden- 46

tifying and building structured models with these groups in mind is important for understanding how 47

variation in exposure or susceptibility and social disparities are interconnected. These models are 48

also useful for designing interventions that can both reduce disparities and disrupt overall trans- 49

mission by focusing efforts on groups most affected by high transmission rates [8, 9]. Transmission 50

models in this space have incorporated subpopulation structure by focusing primarily on accounting 51

for variation in susceptibility and exposure by age [3, 10, 11]. Supporting this approach, susceptibil- 52

ity to infection, contact rates, and cumulative incidence in some locations all appear to vary by age 53

Substantial racial and ethnic disparities in infection rates, hospitalizations, and deaths have been 57

characterized across the US [18–24], but it is unclear how these heterogeneities in risk are expected 58

to change over time, and what implications – if any – they have on overall epidemic dynamics. Here, 59

we aim to address these questions by ﬁtting compartmental SEIR transmission models structured 60

by race and ethnicity to seroprevalence data from New York City and Long Island [16]. We focus pri- 61

marily on building and analyzing variable exposure models because observed disparities in infection 62

rates in US cities are strongly attributable to differences in mobility and exposure [25–27]. Because 63

of the challenges in acquiring racial and ethnic COVID-19 data [28], including social contact data 64

that can be used in transmission models, we analyze a range of model structures that are compati- 65

ble with the data and assess how these assumptions affect estimates of HITs, ﬁnal epidemic sizes, 66

and longitudinal trends in risk across groups. These results highlight the importance of develop- 67

ing socially-informed COVID-19 transmission models that incorporate patterns of epidemic spread 68

across racial and ethnic groups. 69

Calculating the HIT and ﬁnal epidemic size 133

We deﬁned the herd immunity threshold (HIT) for all models as the fraction of non-susceptible peo- 134

ple when the effective reproduction number Rt ﬁrst crosses 1. In the homogenous model, where 135

Rt = Stβ/γ, the analytical solution for the HIT occurs when the fraction of non-susceptible indi- 136

viduals equals 1-1/R0. In the structured models of heterogeneous populations, the HIT was calcu- 137

lated via simulation: we took the dominant eigenvalue of Gt at each timestep to calculate Rt, and 138

identiﬁed the number of non-susceptible individuals when Rt ﬁrst decreased below 1. For the het- 139

erogeneous models with mitigation measures, Rt was calculated at each timestep with respect to 140

the corresponding unmitigated epidemic; in other words, the mitigation scaling factor α was not in- 141

cluded in the Rt calculation. This identiﬁes the point in the epidemic trajectory at which the popu- 142

lation reaches the HIT even if all mitigation measures were lifted (i.e. HIT due to population immu- 143

nity), as opposed to the point in the trajectory when the population transiently reaches the HIT due 144

to mitigation measures (see Supplementary Figure 17 for further explanation). 145

Final epidemic sizes were calculated by simulation by running the epidemic out to 1 year for R0 146

above 2, and 4 years for R0 below 2 to allow additional time for the slower epidemics to fully resolve. 147

The ﬁnal time point was used as the estimate for the ﬁnal epidemic size. 148

Results 203

We model the dynamics of COVID-19 infection allowing for social exposure to infection to vary across 204

racial and ethnic groups. Models incorporating variable susceptibility to COVID-19 are commonly 205

used when stratifying by age because children are thought to have decreased susceptibility to in- 206

fection [10]. Variable susceptibility to infection across racial and ethnic groups has been less well 207

characterized, and observed disparities in infection rates can already be largely explained by differ- 208

ences in mobility and exposure [25–27], likely attributable to social factors such as structural racism 209

that have put racial and ethnic minorities in disadvantaged positions (e.g., employment as frontline 210

workers and residence in overcrowded, multigenerational homes) [35–38]. In line with the notion 211

that variation in exposure could instead be the main driver of observed seroprevalence differences, 212

our primary focus is on analyzing variable exposure models; we have also analyzed variable sus- 213

ceptibility models for comparison (see Supplementary Information). 214

The simplest variable exposure models assume proportionate mixing, where the contact rate be- 215

tween groups is set to be proportional to the total contact rates (i.e., total number of contacts per 216

Discussion 319

Here, we explored how incorporating heterogeneity in SARS-CoV-2 spread across racial and eth- 320

nic groups could affect epidemic dynamics using deterministic transmission models. Models incor- 321

porating variable exposure generally decreased the HIT and ﬁnal epidemic size, but incorporating 322

preferential within-group contacts shifted HITs and ﬁnal epidemic sizes higher, approaching the ho- 323

mogeneous case. Epidemiological measures of disease burden such as incidence rate ratios and 324

cumulative incidence ratios also changed substantially over the course of the epidemic, highlighting 325

the need to account for these trends when evaluating interventions [43]. These results illustrate the 326

varied effects of different structured heterogeneity models, but are not meant to be best estimates 327

given the limited seroprevalence data. 328

Across all model variants, the observed higher cumulative incidence among Hispanics or Latinos 329

and non-Hispanic Black people compared to non-Hispanic whites led to estimates of higher esti- 330

mated contacts relative to non-Hispanic whites, mirroring existing inequities in housing, education, 331

healthcare, and beyond [20, 38, 46–48]. The estimated contact rate differences also concord with 332

The assortativity we observed in the census data has root causes in many areas, including residen- 335

the epidemic forward indicated that the overall HIT was reached after cumulative incidence had in- 337

of achieving herd immunity through infection. All of these factors underscore the fact that incorpo- 339

a homogeneous mixing model; incorporating heterogeneity lowers the HIT but increases it for the 343

highest-risk groups (Figure 2). 344

These results also suggest that public health interventions for reducing COVID-19 inequities can 345

have synergistic effects for controlling the overall epidemic [34]. For instance, from a transmission- 346

control perspective, age-structured models indicate that vaccination of high-contact age groups – 347

such as young adults – is optimal for controlling the spread of SARS-CoV-2 [9]. Similar interven- 348

tions are being explored for disadvantaged populations because of how increased exposure un- 349

derlies much of the higher infection risk that racial and ethnic minorities experience. For instance, 350

Mulberry et al. used a structured SEIR model to evaluate the impact of preferentially vaccinating 351

essential workers, ﬁnding that such a strategy was more effective in reducing morbidity, mortality, 352

and economic cost due to COVID-19 compared to age-only vaccination prioritization strategies [52]. 353

Because racial and ethnic minorities are overrepresented among essential workers [25, 27, 49], fur- 354

ther modeling studies could evaluate the impact of such strategies on also reducing inequities in 355

COVID-19 infection rates. Wrigley-Field et al. took a different methodological approach, projecting 356

demographically-stratiﬁed death rates from 2020 into 2021 assuming various vaccination strategies 357

[53]. In line with the prior study, they found that vaccination strategies that prioritized geographic ar- 358

eas based on socioeconomic criteria or prior COVID mortality rates outperformed age-based strate- 359

gies in reducing overall mortality and inequities in mortality. Because populations here were con- 360

sidered independently, these results could be extended using a transmission modeling framework, 361

such as the one we have described, that accounts for interactions between racial and ethnic groups 362

and thus allows for synergistic beneﬁts from vaccinating high-risk populations. All policy proposals 363

in this space should, of course, carefully consider the legal and ethical dimensions of vaccinations 364

We note several limitations with this study. First, biases in the serosurvey sampling process can 366

substantially affect downstream results; any conclusions drawn depend heavily on the degree to 367

which serosurvey design and post-survey adjustments yield representative samples [55]. For in- 368

stance, because the serosurvey we relied on primarily sampled people at grocery stores, there is 369

both survival bias (cumulative incidence estimates do not account for people who have died) and 370

ascertainment bias (undersampling of at-risk populations that are more likely to self-isolate, such 371

as the elderly) [16, 56]. These biases could affect model estimates if, for instance, the capacity to 372

self-isolate varies by race or ethnicity – as suggested by associations of neighborhood-level mobil- 373

ity versus demographics [27, 57] – leading to an overestimate of cumulative incidence and contact 374

rates in whites. Other sources of uncertainty, such as antibody test sensitivity and speciﬁcity, could 375

also be incorporated into transmission models in future work [56, 58]. Second, we have assumed 376

that seropositivity implies complete immunity and that immunity does not wane. These are strong 377

assumptions that can be revisited as empirical studies on the length of natural immunity are con- 378

ducted. Third, we have assumed the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions such as stay-at- 379

home policies, closures, and the like to equally affect racial and ethnic groups. Empirical evidence 380

suggests that during periods of lockdown, certain neighborhoods that are disproportionately wealthy 381

and white tend to show greater declines in mobility than others [27, 57]. These simplifying assump- 382

tions were made to aid in illustrating the key ﬁndings of this model, but for more detailed predictive 383

models, the extent to which contact rate differences change could be evaluated using longitudinal 384

contact survey data [59], since granular mobility data are typically not stratiﬁed by race and ethnicity 385

due to privacy concerns [60]. Fourth, due to data availability, we have only considered variability in 386

exposure due to one demographic characteristic; models should ideally strive to also account for the 387

effects of age on susceptibility and exposure within strata of race and ethnicity and other relevant 388

demographics, such as socioeconomic status and occupation [52]. These models could be ﬁt using 389

representative serological studies with detailed cross-tabulated seropositivity estimates. Finally, we 390

have estimated model parameters using a single cross-sectional serosurvey. To improve estimates 391

and the ability to distinguish between model structures, future studies should use longitudinal sero- 392

surveys or case data stratiﬁed by race and ethnicity and corrected for underreporting; the challenge 393

will be ensuring that such data are systematically collected and made publicly available, which has 394

been a persistent barrier to research efforts [28]. Addressing these data barriers will also be key 395

for translating these and similar models into actionable policy proposals on vaccine distribution and 396

dynamics of infection in racial and ethnic groups, and how the impact of heterogeneity on the HIT 399

and ﬁnal epidemic size depends strongly on the details of how heterogeneity is modeled. We have 400

shown that due to early infections in individuals from the most at-risk groups, relative measures of 401

incidence may decline and even reverse, but inequities in the cumulative burden of infection persist 402

throughout the epidemic as the HIT is reached. These results describe a framework that can be ex- 403

tended to other cities and countries in which racial and ethnic disparities in seropositivity have been 404

observed [17, 61, 62] and are a step towards using transmission models to design policy interven- 405

Variable susceptibility versus variable exposure models 413

The serosurvey data were compatible with variable susceptibility models in which Hispanics or Lati- 414

nos, non-Hispanic Black people, non-Hispanic Asians, and multiracial or other people had 2.25, 415

1.62, 0.86, and 1.28 times the susceptibility to infection relative to non-Hispanic whites in NYC, re- 416

spectively, and 4.32, 1.96, 0.92, and 2.48 times the susceptibility to infection relative to non-Hispanic 417

whites in Long Island, respectively. As with variable exposure models, these differences in suscep- 418

tibility lowered herd immunity levels and ﬁnal epidemic sizes relative to the homogeneous model 419

(Supplementary Figure 1), but to a lesser extent; for instance, variable susceptibility models resulted 420

in HITs ∼10% greater than HITs under proportionate mixing for Long Island. 421

The difference between these models is that incorporating heterogeneity in susceptibility only af- 422

fects susceptible individuals, but heterogeneity in exposure impacts both susceptible and infectious 423

individuals: individuals from racial and ethnic groups with higher contact rates are both more likely 424

to be infected, and when infected, to infect a greater number of secondary cases. This contrast is 425

clear when comparing the next-generation matrices for each model, which lists the average number 426

of secondary infections caused by an infected individual from a given demographic group (Supple- 427

mentary Figures 2 and 3). The epidemic resolves at an earlier stage in variable exposure models 428

once these key transmission groups become immune because of this additional compound effect on 429

transmission. 430

Our results contrasting mechanistic variable exposure and susceptibility models are in line with the- 431

oretical studies, which also indicate that models incorporating heterogeneity in exposure have more 432

pronounced effects on HITs than models incorporating heterogeneity in susceptibility, assuming 433

comparable continuous distributions of exposure and susceptibility [4, 6]. Tkachenko et al. showed 434

that the HIT = 1 −(1/R0)(1/λ), where λ is either 1 + CV 2 for variable susceptibility models or 435

1 + CV 2(2 + γsCV )/(1 + CV 2) for variable exposure models, and CV is the coefﬁcient of variation 436

and γs is the skewness for the exposure distribution [6]. We calculated CV and skewness using the 437

susceptibility and total contact rate ratios and substituted those values into the HIT formula, which 438

is an approximation because our exposure and susceptibility distributions are discrete; nonetheless, 439

the approximations result in similar HIT curves to the simulation results (Supplementary Figure 4). 440
